title: Larsen's Opening: 1.b3
description: A fun, offbeat opening best suited for players who like crazy positions. Better beyond the beginner level.

r1b1k1nr/2p1q2p/p1pb1pp1/3p4/5P1Q/1PN5/P.text:
And face a check on e7.

This move is designed to disrupt our development, as we probably wanted to activate the knight to f3.

Now it's going to block the check on e2.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1n2p/p1nb2p1/1B1pp3/7Q/1PN1P.text: Once the bishop is attacked, you don't have to take in this line.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1n2p/p1nb2p1/3pp3/7Q/1PN1P3/.text:
It's better to retreat and keep the bishop for a possible kingside attack.

Black will struggle to come up with a sound plan here while we prepare the attack. 

We will play Nf3 and g4 next.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1n2p/2nb2p1/1B1pp3/7Q/1PN1P3.text:
Black castles...

And so will we, but on the queenside.

r1bqk1nr/1pp3pp/p1nb1p2/1B1pp3/5P2/1PN1P.text:
Black pushing the a-pawn here is rare (only 7%) but has some merit to it in the sense that Black gets rid of one of our troublemakers.

We will capture on c6.

No point in retreating, and this way we also double Black's pawns.

r1bqk1nr/2p3pp/p1pb1p2/3pp3/5P2/1PN1P3/P.text:
Black recaptures.

Let's begin kingside operations now.

We'll give a check on h5.

This forces Black to weaken their position.

r1bqk1nr/2p4p/p1pb1pp1/3p4/5p1Q/1PN1P3/P.text:
Black finally takes on f4, in hopes of developing with tempo just like we did.

We'll take back...

r1bqk1nr/2p4p/p1pb1pp1/3pp2Q/5P2/1PN1P3/.text:
They will most likely block with a pawn.

Now we can slide to h4 and keep the queen active, while preparing to castle queenside.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2nb4/1B1pp3/8/1P2P3/PBP.text:
Black will defend with the bishop more than half the time, as it is logical to develop while protecting the pawn.

But the downside of that move is that it leaves the g7-pawn undefended, so we can immediately attack on the flank!

If they don't know the theory, this position must not feel comfortable.

r1bqk1nr/ppp3pp/2nb1p2/1B1pp3/5P2/1P2P3/.text:
The main move is actually 5...f6, as ugly as it looks. It's played just over 30% of the time.

This creates some light-squared weaknesses which we might later use.

First, we will develop and attack the d5-pawn as well.

Of course, we didn't want to capture on e5 and leave Black with a strong center and room to develop the knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp1n1pp/2nb1p2/1B1pp3/5P2/1PN1P.text:
Expect to see ...Ne7 almost half the time as it is the most common move here.

We don't want to give Black too much room to breathe, so we will take in the center.

Our main idea is to use the light-squared diagonal and develop the queen with tempo.

This will both allow us to castle quickly and weaken Black's pawn structure, creating more weaknesses.

r1bqk2r/ppp1n1pp/2nb4/1B1pp3/8/1PN1P3/PB.text:
Black recaptures with the pawn.

Recapturing with the bishop is also possible, and it's played a quarter of the time.

In that case, our plan is simple: Qh5+ and Qf3 to prevent Black from castling.

In this case, we will still give this check. Black can't block with the knight because of the hanging d5-pawn, of course.

r1bqk2r/ppp1n2p/2nb2p1/1B1pp2Q/8/1PN1P3/.text:
So they block with the pawn.

Now we can slide back to h4 and keep the queen on the kingside, awaiting other pieces.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pp3/8/1P2P3/PBPP1P.text:
Black places both pawns in the center. Now, how can we reintroduce the threat of capturing the e5-pawn?

Sure, we can attack it with the knight, but then Black could push ...e4.

Instead, we can pin the defender of the pawn! Now the knight can't move and we are threatening to take on e5 again.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP.text:
2...Nc6, developing the knight and protecting the center, is played 55% of the time.

Our main ideas will revolve around harassing the e5-pawn, as I mentioned.

I prefer e3 to e4 because it gives us flexibility to push f4 later, which
we will want to do, as you will see.

r2qk1nr/1pp4p/p1nbbpp1/1B1pp3/5P1Q/1PN1P.text:
Instead, White attacks our bishop.

But we will keep the momentum by capturing on c6.

r2qk1nr/2p4p/p1pbbpp1/3pp3/5P1Q/1PN1P3/P.text:
And we can simply castle now, having almost completed our development.

The knight will come out next.

r2qk1nr/p1p2b1p/2pb2p1/3pp3/6Q1/1PN1P3/P.text:
This doubles Black's c-pawns...

Which we can immediately attack with the queen!

Our queen is pressuring the c6-pawn and pinning it at the same time.

r2qk1nr/ppp2b1p/2nb1pp1/1B1pp3/5PQ1/1PN1.text:
So they push it.

We got what we wanted.

Now I suggest a series of trades that improve our position and target Black's weaknesses.

First, let's take in the center.

r2qk1nr/ppp2b1p/2nb2p1/1B1pp3/6Q1/1PN1P3.text:
Black recaptures with the pawn to maintain the center.

Now we can capture the knight as well.

r2qk1nr/ppp2bpp/2nb1p2/1B1pp2Q/5P2/1PN1P.text:
Black doesn't have to play ...g6 when they can put a bishop on f7.

They keep their pawn structure intact for now.

In fact, let's provoke ...g6 again by attacking the g7-pawn.

Black doesn't have a good way of protecting it.

r2qk1nr/ppp3pp/2nbbp2/1B1pp3/5P2/1PN1P3/.text:
6...Be6 is played almost 30% of the time and is another way of protecting the d5-pawn.

Black's pieces certainly do look a bit cramped together, though.

We'll still play Qh5+.

It's important to get the queen out with check.

r2qk1nr/ppp4p/2nbbpp1/1B1pp2Q/5P2/1PN1P3.text:
If Black pushes ...g6, we can simply slide to the h4-square.

From there we put pressure on the f6-pawn and disallow the knight to develop to e7.

r2qk2r/p1p1nb1p/2pb2p1/3pp3/Q7/1PN1PN2/P.text:
We can comfortably develop the knight and aim for the g5-square.

It would be great if we could trade for that bishop and capture on d5 since the c6-pawn is pinned.

Also, we'll castle kingside here and have an open f-file for the rook.

White is doing great.

r3k1nr/2p1q2p/p1pb1pp1/3p1b2/5P1Q/1PN5/P.text:
And we'll castle.

White is clearly better here, having finished development and castled while Black is struggling to get the knight into the game.

We've got a lot of potential on the e-file and in the center, and can also play against Black's doubled c-pawns down the line.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/8/1P6/P1PPPPPP/R.text:
As with most early fianchetto setups, we give the other side freedom to play in the center.

The most common move after 1.b3 is 1...e5, played almost 30% of the time in more than 24 million games.

We'll fianchetto our bishop and attack the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to our course on 1.b3 for White!

In this chapter, we will start with the theoretically most standard line: Black playing 1...e5 on the first move. 

We will start with 1.b3.

We want to activate the dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal and then attack the center quickly.

2kr2nB/p1p4p/2pb1p2/3p3q/6b1/1P2PN1P/P1P.text:
Now we are actually threatening to capture the bishop on g4, so Black will have to move it.

After that, we will finish development, trade some pieces if we can and enjoy a winning position up the exchange, since Black will most likely capture our bishop on h8.

r1b1k1nr/ppp1q1pp/2nb1p2/1B1pp3/5P2/1P2P.text:
A move that could hold the game  for now is ...f6.

Black is investing all their forces into protecting that pawn.

We won't stop attacking.

One of the best things about the b3-setups is that you can often activate pieces with tempi because Black's position is stuck together, trying to defend.

r1b1k1nr/ppp1qppp/2nb4/1B1pp3/5P2/1P2P3/.text:
Black defends the pawn with the queen a quarter of the time.

It doesn't lose for now, but Black can easily get into a lost position just by playing natural moves in these lines.

We will add another attacker to the pawn.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2pBp/2nb4/1B1p4/5p1q/1P2P3/P.text:
Black gives the check.

Their main point is that we can't play g3, so we have to move the king.

But that's completely fine.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2pBp/2nb4/1B1p4/7q/1P2p3/P1P.text:
Sure enough, Black will get a lot of activity and pressure in this line, but we will be able to defend.

Here, they take on e3 and the bishop is coming to g4.

Checkmate is also threatened.

Let's recapture on e3.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2nb4/1B1p4/5p2/1P2P3/PB.text:
Black could try and capture here, giving up the g7-pawn.

They might think they can get sufficient compensation for the loss of material after ...Qh4+.

But if we know how to defend, we are winning. And this move is played 20% of the time, which is a lot for a losing mistake.

We'll accept their sacrifice. The rook will be lost too.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2nb4/1B1pp3/8/1P2P3/PBP.text:
Black defends.

But leaves themselves open for a flank attack.

r1bqkbnr/1pp3pp/p1n2p2/1B1p4/2PPp3/1P2P3.text:
The only way to get a pawn to c6 is to attack our bishop.

We'll capture.

r1bqkbnr/2p3pp/p1p2p2/3p4/2PPp3/1P2P3/PB.text:
And we have a clear plan of harassing the d5-pawn in this scenario.

We will do that with the two knights: on f4 and on c3.

And sure, Black defends d5 with a pawn, but this is not the same.

Black's pawn structure is much weaker now.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pp3/8/1P2P3/PBPP1P.text:
Black places both pawns in the center.

We'll pin the knight and threaten to capture on e5 again.

Let's look at some other options here for Black.

For example, ...Bd7 is played in roughly 20% of games, but doesn't need to be analyzed here as it simply loses a pawn.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n2p2/1B1p4/3Pp3/1P2P3/P.text:
Instead, they might push ...e4 here and try to grab more space.

We'll respond with c4 to continue our central aggression.

Black can't play ...c6 to create a pawn chain because they already committed with the knight.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n2p2/1B1pp3/8/1P2P3/PBP.text:
Black could preemptively play ...f6 here instead of ...Bd6, although it looks dubious to block the knight this early.

It's played 6% of the time.

Since f4 isn't powerful anymore, let's change things up a bit.

The e3-pawn also supports the d4-square, not just the f4-square!

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP.text:
The knight defends.

We'll open up the bishop.

It's coming to b5.

r3k1nB/p1p4p/2pb1p2/3p3q/6b1/1P2PN2/P1P3.text:
Black goes for ...f6 to trap our bishop.

It won't be able to get out, but that's fine.

We'll attack the bishop with h3.

For now, we aren't actually threatening to capture it because of the h-pawn being pinned.

r3k1nr/1pp1q1pp/p1nbbp2/1B1pp3/5P2/1PN1P.text:
For example, ...a6 already gives us a big advantage.

We will take on c6 and begin a tactical combination.

r3k1nr/2p1q1pp/p1p1b3/3pb3/8/1PN1P3/PBPP.text:
Why?

Because we have this check with a fork.

r3k1nr/2p1q1pp/p1p5/3pQ3/8/1PN1P3/PBPP2P.text:
If Black blocks with the queen, it's even worse.

Because we can capture on d5 with the knight!

If Black takes the knight on d5, we have Qxg7.

r3k1nr/2p1q1pp/p1pbb3/3pp3/8/1PN1PN2/PBP.text:
Why are we making these trades?

Well, we can sacrifice the knight here!

We had to capture on c6 to remove the defender of the e5-square first.

Now this tactic works.

r3k1nr/2p1q1pp/p1pbbp2/3pp3/5P2/1PN1PN2/.text:
Black recaptures.

Now we will take on e5.

r3k1nr/2p1qbpp/p1p5/3pb2Q/8/1PN1P3/PBPP2.text:
But what if Black retreats with the bishop, attacks our queen and defends?

This is where our castling idea comes into play.

We will sacrifice the rook!

The best move for Black is 13...Bxh2+. We would recapture with the queen in that case.

r3k1nr/2p2qpp/p1p5/3pb2Q/8/1PN1P3/PBPP2P.text:
But if they take the rook, we're winning.

We are still down the exchange, but this is not the end of our tactical power in this position.

r3k1nr/2p3Bp/p7/3p4/8/1P2P3/P1PP2PP/R5K1.text:
And that's because we will win the rook back, and Black won't be able to trap our bishop and capture it.

So we will be equal in pieces, but we will be up 3 pawns in total.

That makes for a completely winning position.

r3k1nr/2p3pp/p1p5/3Nq3/8/1P2P3/PBPP2PP/R.text:
They can trade the queens first.

But bishops move diagonally too!

And now there is the additional threat of Nc7+ with a fork.

r3k1nr/2p3pp/p7/3pB3/8/1P2P3/P1PP2PP/R5K.text: Taking here doesn't work for the same reason as before.

r3k1nr/p1p2pBp/2pb4/3p3q/6b1/1P2PN2/P1P3.text:
This battery isn't dangerous at all.

We have defended sufficiently.

It's time to capture the rook in the corner.

r3k1nr/p1p2pBp/2pb4/3p4/6bq/1P2P3/P1P3PP.text:
Black recaptures.

And now we'll block with the knight, counterattacking Black's queen.

r3k1nr/ppp1q1pp/2nbbp2/1B1pp3/5P2/1PN1PN.text:
They don't have many choices but to defend with the bishop here.

We'll simply castle. You will see why this move is important soon.

Black will have to be extremely accurate not to lose the game here.

r3k1nr/ppp1qppp/2nb4/1B1pp3/5Pb1/1P2PN2/.text:
Black can pin our knight on f3.

Seems natural, right?

We'll castle.

r3k1nr/ppp2pBp/2nb4/1B1p4/6bq/1P2P3/P1P3.text:
Black activates the bishop now and  attacks our queen.

Before we play Nf3 to block, we don't want Black's knight interfering with our defense in the future.

So we will get rid of it first.

We will be up material anyway, so trading pieces is good.

r3k2r/ppp1qppp/2n2n2/1B1pB3/8/1P2Pb2/P1P.text:
So they capture on f3.

But we won't just recapture and allow Black to take on e5.

This is why the knight being on f6 loses the game.

We can take the knight and counterattack the queen!

r3k2r/ppp1qppp/2n2n2/1B1pb3/6b1/1P2PN2/P.text:
Recapturing on e5 doesn't work.

Black gets into a trading skirmish that wins for us.

We'll take on e5.

Of course, Black can't take with the queen now.

r3k2r/ppp1qppp/2nb1n2/1B1pp3/5Pb1/1P2PN2.text:
And Black activates the knight to f6.

Also seems natural. But it loses the game!

The point is that the knight being on f6 allows us to capture on e5 with the pawn.

r3k2r/ppp2Qpp/2n5/1B1p4/8/1P2P3/P1PP2PP/.text:
Well, that was a trap.

We can take on f7 with check and we are completely winning.

After ...Kd8, we will play Nc3 and attack the queen after which we can take on d5 or on g7.

Everything wins.

r3k2r/ppp2ppp/2n2q2/1B1p4/8/1P2Pb2/P1PP2.text:
Black doesn't want to trade queens and takes.

We'll recapture the bishop.

We calculated everything correctly, right?

We didn't hang a piece or anything.

r3k2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B1p4/8/1P2PQ2/P1PP2PP.text: Oh, but the rook on a1 was hanging!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/8/1P6/P1PPPPPP/R.text:
Black advances in the center.

We'll fianchetto and attack the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Study 2 of the first chapter will show us Black's alternatives to 5...f6 on move 5.

They can choose to protect the pawn with the queen, as you will see, which already leads to a comfortable position where Black can easily slip and lose the game!

Apart from that, they can also try and capture on f4, giving up the rook and trying to find some compensation.

r1b1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/5q2/2p5/4p3/1P2P3/P1PP.text:
The queen recaptures and now our rook is under attack.

We'll block with the knight, attacking the e4-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/8/2p1q3/4p3/1PN1P3/P1P.text: Black keeps the queen on the diagonal and protects the pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/8/2p1q3/4pP2/1PN1P3/P1.text:
But we'll play f4 to retain the initiative.

We don't mind Black taking en passant as that would activate our queen.

Black will probably have to retreat and try to hold on to the pawn, all the while not being able to play ...d5.

Winning tempi like this, and now being able to play d3 as well, is why giving up the bishop is good.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/5q2/2p5/2PpN3/1P2P3/P2P1.text:
Simply capture on e4 and you're fine.

You can continue development on light squares with Bd3 and/or Qf3.

If Black captures on e3, it's better to recapture with the d-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/5q2/2p5/2p1p3/1PN1P3/P2P.text:
Capturing on c4 is an option, although it looks unorthodox to split the pawns like this.

We'll recapture and keep the attack on e4.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/5q2/2pp4/2P1p3/1P2P3/P2P.text:
The queen recaptures.

Our rook is under attack.

But we'll block with the knight, just like the 6...c5 line.

Black has to worry about their over-extended center now.

r1bq1rk1/p1p2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4p3/1P2P3/PBP.text:
The point is to split Black's pawns even more.

Look at the pawn islands on the queenside now.

We'll prepare castling with no problems in the position.

Apart from the bad structure, the e4-pawn is overextended and could become a target.

Also, our bishop on b2 is much better than Black's bishop on c5.

r1bq1rk1/p1p2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4p3/1PN1P3/PB.text:
And ruin their pawn structure.

Now trading queens is beneficial for us.

r1bq1rk1/p1p2ppp/2p2n2/2bp4/4p3/1P1PP3/P.text:
Still, it's stable for now, so Black castles.

We'll take once.

r1bq1rk1/p1p2ppp/2p2n2/2bp4/4p3/1PNPP3/P.text:
They choose to support it with ...d5, creating a pawn chain.

That won't help them in the long run.

We'll take once.

r1bq1rk1/p1p2ppp/2pb1n2/3p4/4P3/1P2P3/PB.text:
And we'll take in the center.

Black has to be careful here.

9...Nxe4 gives us a big advantage after 10.Nxe4 dxe4 11.Qd4.

9...dxe4 allows Nc4 or even the comfortable Be2.

The best course of action for Black is probably ...Re8.

r1bq1rk1/p1pp1ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4p3/1P1PP3/P.text:
Black could recapture with the b-pawn.

We don't have to activate the knight to d2 now.

We can be even more active with Nc3, targeting the center.

Black has to react to the threats on the e4-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/4p3/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
They castle.

This does nothing to stop d4.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/8/2PPp3/1PN1PN2.text:
Pushing ...e4 isn't the best alternative for Black.

They won't be able to protect the pawn with ...d5 next.

So the e4-pawn is just a target.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/8/2Pp4/1PN1PN2/.text:
Taking is natural.

I actually recommend against recapturing with the pawn and opening up the e-file before we castle.

Let's take with the knight instead and activate it in the center, provoking Black to trade.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/8/2PQ4/1PN1P3/PB.text:
But with the queen.

The bishop is coming to e2 next and we can choose which way we want to castle.

It's important to note that Black plays ...c5 here 33% of the time, and it's a big positional mistake.

It leaves a big hole on the d5-square and weakens the d6-pawn.

What Black should instead do is play ...Be6 and play for ...d5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/8/2Pn4/1PN1P3/PB.text:
And they do.

Again, we won't recapture with the pawn.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4p3/1P1PP3/PB.text:
It's more natural for Black to take with the d-pawn.

We'll continue with our plan.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/3Np3/1P1PP3/.text:
Castling is most common.

Now we'll take because we are in time to play Nd2.

r1bqk2r/p1p2ppp/2p2n2/2bp4/4p3/1P1PP3/PB.text:
This forces Black to recapture with the b-pawn and reach a structure that's much worse than the one they would have gotten had they recaptured with the d-pawn.

The c-pawns are doubled and the a7-pawn is isolated.

Meanwhile, we can continue with natural development.

The center is under pressure.

r1bqk2r/p1p2ppp/2pb1n2/3p4/4p3/1P1PP3/PB.text:
Black doesn't want to weaken their pawns and make our development easier, so they play ...Bd6.

Having created some tension in the center, it's time to pile up on it.

The knight coming to d2 is very common in these types of positions.

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/4p3/2P5/1P2PN2/P.text:
Black could go for simple development here and prepare castling.

We'll continue development as well, with d4 incoming as Black has chosen a more passive route.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/1b6/3p4/3Pn3/1P1B4/PBP2P.text:
But our position is comfortable after O-O.

Natural improving moves like Nd2 and Re1 are coming if Black plays the natural ...O-O.

Otherwise, Black could try and be aggressive with ...Qg5, in which case you could even choose a setup with c4 and Nc3 to target the center.
Black can expand in the center and defend.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/2bp4/3Np3/1P1PP3/P.text:
The move ...d5 is a sensible option to come at any point.

Black simply strengthens the center.

However, the d-pawn left its post on d7, so we'll capture on c6.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1b3n2/8/3Pp3/1P1P4/PBP2.text:
Plus, we won a tempo.

Black has to retreat to the b6-square.

Which gives us time to capture in the center.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1b6/8/3Pn3/1P6/PBP2PPP/.text:
Black recaptures, and do you see another developing move that comes with an attack on one of Black's pieces?

Sometimes, the positions just play themselves.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/3Np3/1P2P3/PB.text:
5...Bc5 puts more pressure on the knight, but we don't have to worry about that.

Focusing on the center proves to be much more effective.

So we'll challenge the e4-pawn and prepare Nd2.

As in many lines in this study, the knight is better on d2 than on c3 because it doesn't block the bishop on b2 but still controls some key squares.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/2b5/3np3/1P1PP3/PBP.text:
Black can choose to trade now.

We don't want to trade off our dark-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/2p2n2/3p4/4p3/1P2P3/PBP.text:
Black has to recapture with the b-pawn.

This could lead to their pawn structure being weak in the long run.

We have to challenge the center now.

And we can do that with d3.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/5n2/2p5/3Bp3/1P2P3/P1P.text:
Black wants to grab a tempo and expand with ...c5, but it won't work.

We won't just retreat blindly.

In fact, we'll capture on f6!

I'll explain why we made this trade shortly.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/2pp4/2PBp3/1P2P3/P2P.text:
A more active alternative is ...c5, attacking our bishop.

It's important to know what to do here.

If we just retreat, ...d4 is coming.

We have to keep the momentum and capture.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3p4/3Np3/1P2P3/PB.text:
The move ...d5 could arrive now.

Usually, when you see this move, capturing on c6 is a good idea.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/4p3/8/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
Black goes for 4...d6 34% of the time, protecting the center.

The main downside is that the bishop on f8 is blocked.

Since Black has taken over the dark squares with the pawns, we'll compensate on the light squares.

It's important to establish control of the d5-square.

We will be playing for d4 eventually.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/3Bp3/1P2P3/P1PP.text:
A better alternative than ...c5 is definitely ...d5.

Black solidifies the center.

But not for long.

It's important to challenge the center right away.

If Black defends with ...c6, we're happy and can continue with Nc3.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/8/1P2P3/PBPP.text:
In more than 1.4 million games in the database, Black played ...Nf6 on move 3, reaching the Two Knights setup.

The frequency of this move is 22%.

Black plays a flexible developing move and leaves their options open for central expansion and further development.

We'll continue by attacking the pawn.

It's interesting that ...d5 and ...Bc5 in this position take up 30% of all moves, and they obviously drop the e5-pawn! Very careless!

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/4p3/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
Black pushes ...e4 17% of the time.

It certainly looks logical to grab some more central space with tempo.

However, that gives us mobility on the dark squares and the long diagonal.

We'll escape to the center and try to undermine the e4-pawn in the long run.

There's tension between the knights now.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/3np3/1P2P3/PBPP1.text:
Of course, you should expect Black to take on d4 at a certain frequency.

It's logical to recapture with the bishop and keep it active, and the pawns together.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP.text:
Black defends and develops the queen's knight.

We'll continue on the dark squares.

r1br2k1/p1p2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4p3/1PN1P3/PBP.text:
The point is that we're closer to the endgame without the queens on the board, and considering the pawn structures, we would definitely have an advantage in the endgame.

Here, we'll castle on the next move and bring the rooks to the center.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/4p3/2P3b1/1P2PN2.text:
And so will Black.

Now that the knight is fine, we can continue with our expansion.

d4 is coming.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/5b2/2PPp3/1PN1P3.text: They can defend it for now, but their pieces are tied down to the pawn.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/5b2/2PPp3/PPN1P3.text:
Meanwhile, we have an easy plan to continue.

We'll start with a3 to prevent any ...Nb4 ideas.

Then, our bishop is coming to e2 and we'll make use of Black's vulnerable pieces to play g4 and h4 and try to dislodge them while expanding.

White is better.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/8/2PN4/1P2P3/PB2.text:
We can recapture with the queen.

We have various plans: Nxc6, damaging Black's structure is a viable option.

If we want more of a queenside approach, our knight can come to d5 via c3 to try and open up the c-file after a trade.

The bishop on b2 is a useful attacking piece, on the other hand.

Either way, good improving moves are Rac1, Rfd1 and Qf3.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/8/2Pp2b1/1P2PN2/.text:
Black takes.

As in the 5...Be7 line, we'll recapture with the knight.

This also keeps our bishop on b2 active.

There's tension between the light-squared bishops now.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b2b2/4p3/1P1PP3/P.text:
The bishop comes out to protect the center.

Black is threatening to capture on d3 now.

So we'll take first.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b2B2/8/1P2P3/PBPn1P.text:
We'll take on f5 instead, and the knight on d2 is trapped!

...Qg5 is met with Bd3, and the best Black can do is an absurd engine combination that still gives us a big advantage:

11...Qg5 12.Bd3 Bxe3 13.fxe3 Qxg2 14.Qxd2 Qxh1+ 15.Bf1.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b2b2/4n3/1P2P3/PBPN.text:
The knight recaptures.

It seems like Black is applying a lot of pressure, but we're completely fine.

In fact, Black has to be careful here after we play Bd3.

The knight on e4 is under attack twice, and the bishop on f5 is undefended, too.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b2b2/8/1P1BP3/PBPn1.text:
For example, capturing on d2 is a mistake.

We won't just recapture and allow Black to do what they want.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/4p3/2P3b1/1P2PN2/.text:
An active move that actually addresses our plans is ...Bg4.

Black pins our knight and makes d4 harder to play, for now.

Of course, we'll unpin immediately.

We don't want ...e4 to come, even though we would survive it.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/5q2/1Bp2b2/4p3/1PN1P3/P2P1.text:
But is in some trouble after the check on b5, since retreating the bishop to d7 doesn't make sense anymore, so Black will probably have to move the king.

Our plan after that is certainly f3 to undermine the center, as well as castling.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/5q2/2p2b2/2B1p3/1PN1P3/P2P.text: Black can defend with the bishop...

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/8/1P6/P1PPPPPP/R.text:
Black places a pawn in the center.

We'll fianchetto the bishop and attack the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Almost every opening has its own Two Knights variation, and that's the setup we are going to explore in Chapter 2.

Instead of going for the traditional 3...d5, Black opts for 3...Nf6 and claims that activating the knights before anything else is essential.

Let's begin.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1b1p1/3p1n1p/3Pnp2/2P1p3/1PN.text:
And we'll castle long.

Our knight is coming to f4, from where it can either jump to g6 or e6 depending on what we need.

White is doing well.
Black takes control of the g5-square.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1b1pp/3p1n2/3Pnp2/2P1p3/1PN1.text:
The knight does jump to e5, but it doesn't have much potential yet.

We'll activate the queen.

I actually recommend queenside castling because we might be able to attack down the line.

r1bq1rk1/pppnb1pp/3p1n2/3P1p2/2P1p3/1PN1.text:
Black maneuvers as well.

We did give them the e5-square for the knight, so we can expect it to land there.

That's fine. We'll finish development anyway.

r3kbnr/pp5p/2n1bqp1/1B1pQ3/3Pp3/1PN1P3/P.text: Black will block with the knight on c6.

r3kbnr/ppQ4p/2n1bqp1/1B1p4/3Pp3/1PN1P3/P.text:
Now we can avoid the trade productively by placing the queen on c7 and targeting the knight.

If Black plays ...Rc8, we can capture on b7. And moving the bishop drops the d5-pawn.

In fact, it's very hard to defend.

We are on the verge of being winning here.

rn1qkbnr/pp4pp/2p1b3/3p1p2/2PPp3/1PN1PP2.text:
Black really wants to keep everything together.

Let's start capturing.

We trade on d5.

rn1qkbnr/pp4pp/2p1bp2/3p4/2PPp3/1PN1P3/P.text:
The bishop comes to e6 to defend.

It seems like we've hit a dead end with the pressure, but there are other pawn breaks that undermine Black's structure.

In this case, that's f3.

It's extremely important to know how to chip away at certain extended structures like this one not to get suffocated.

rn1qkbnr/pp4pp/4b3/3p1p2/3Pp3/1PN1PP2/PB.text:
Black recaptures.

And now we'll take on e4 as well.

rn1qkbnr/pp4pp/4b3/3p4/3Pp3/1PN1P3/PB4PP.text:
Black takes with the f-pawn, which is more practical.

However, we've got the advantage now.

Because we have this check on h5, and the queen is infiltrating in the center.

rn1qkbnr/pp5p/4b1p1/3p3Q/3Pp3/1PN1P3/PB4.text:
Black blocks with ...g6.

But we'll fork the bishop and the rook on h8.

There's only one move that saves both.

rn2kbnr/pp5p/4bqp1/3pQ3/3Pp3/1PN1P3/PB4P.text:
And that's ...Qf6.

Black is going to be extremely happy if we trade the queens on f6, so we won't do that.

We'll give a check on b5 first.

It's always good to develop with tempo, but there's another reason for this move.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1b1pp/3p1n2/3P1p2/2P1p3/1P2P.text:
Black castles...

And we'll continue with natural development.

We'll activate our pieces on light squares next.

rnbqk2r/ppp1b1pp/3p1n2/3P1p2/2P1p3/1P2P3.text:
Black doesn't have many options at this point.

So they prepare castling.

I suggest we develop our knight to h3. It doesn't have a concrete plan yet, but h3 is still better than g1.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/3p1n2/4pp2/2P5/1P2P3/PB1.text:
The knight arrives at f6.

And we'll go for the central expansion.

It's crucial to challenge Black's center.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/3p1n2/5p2/2PPp3/1P2P3/PB.text:
Black doesn't want to trade but commits the pawn further and claims a space advantage.

We will mirror their move and push our pawn to d5!

We are both restricting each other's pieces, but our bishop on b2 is a monster.

rnbqkbnr/pp4pp/2p2p2/3p4/2PPp3/1P2P3/PB3.text:
Black will most likely defend with ...c6.

Now we can build behind our pawns.

The knight is best on c3, pressuring the center, of course.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP/.text:
Played 20% of the time, ...d6 does defend the pawn.

But it blocks in the dark-squared bishop and gives us a lot of space.

We'll counter Black's pawn chain on the dark squares with c4, dominating the d5-square.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/3p4/4pp2/2P5/1P6/PB1PPPP.text:
You will usually either see the ...d6 and ...f5 setup or the ...f6 and ...d5 setup.

Black has to expand one way or another.

The move e3 is a good response either way, as we will go for d4.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/5p2/3p4/3Pp3/1P2P3/PBP2P.text:
Especially when Black pushes ...e4.

This pawn structure should ring alarm bells, though.

For you to play c4!

This is the best way to fight against the structure and possibly bring our bishop back to life.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/5p2/3pp3/8/1P2P3/PBPP1PP.text:
Black expands in the center as planned.

We don't want to give them too much space, though.

So we'll play d4 and block their advancement while grabbing central space.

This is a commitment because we block our bishop on b2.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/8/1P6/P1PPPPPP/R.text:
Black goes for ...e5.

Let's attack the pawn.

As we know, the most common and the most natural move to defend it is ...Nc6.

However, Black has other options.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/5p2/4p3/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP/.text:
2...f6 is played 5% of the time.

It always looks ugly to play ...f6 this early in the game.

However, Black wants to keep their center protected and play ...d5 at the same time.

There isn't much we can do about the immediate ...d5, so let's just continue with standard improving moves.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
We know that there are many different lines Black can go for in the 1.b3 opening.

In Chapter 3, we will cover the lines with Black avoiding ...Nc6.

In particular, these will be 2...d6 and 2...f6.

2kr3r/ppqnbppp/2p1pnb1/3p4/2P4N/1P1PP1P1.text:
One of them is g3, preemptively acting to contain the queen and the dark-squared bishop's power against our king.

Placing a rook on the c-file is a must, combined with capturing in the center and trying to open up that file.

Our d2-knight can improve on f3.

2kr3r/ppqnbppp/2p1pnb1/3p4/2P4N/1P1PP3/P.text: After Black castles, there are multiple ideas we could go for.

r1b2rk1/ppq1bppp/2n1pn2/2ppN3/5P2/1P1BP3.text:
Black can decline and play ...Qc7.

But now we have a big space advantage.

r1b2rk1/ppq1bppp/2n1pn2/2ppN3/5P2/1P1BPR.text:
We can think about attacking after Rf3, with the idea of Rh3.

The position is equal, but Black has to be careful.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/4p3/2ppP3/6Q1/1P1BP3/P.text:
Now we can play actively with Qg4, and the queen is lurking around Black's king.

The position is still in the balance, but Black could easily mess up if they are not careful. 

For example, Rf3 and Rh3 is interesting to converge on the h7-pawn.

On the queenside, we can consider moves like a4 or c4 and develop the knight.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/4p3/2ppP3/8/1P1BP3/PBP.text:
Which rotates to d7.

We've removed Black's most important defender.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/5P2/1P1BPN2.text:
Black activates their knight to c6, but that won't stop us.

We'll offer the trade anyway.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2ppn3/5P2/1P1BP3/P.text:
Black will most likely trade.

We'll recapture with an attack on the knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/3p4/2PP4/1P2PN2/P.text:
That's c4.

Of course, we don't want to capture and reactivate Black's bishop.

Both sides would rather leave the tension and let the other side capture.

We'll improve behind our structure next with Nbd2 and Bd3, and castle, with a clamp on e5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/3p4/8/1P3N2/PBPP.text:
Black activates both knights, but we've already achieved a small positional victory.

Now we can continue in a natural manner.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/8/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
Going for ...e6 now simply blocks the bishop.

We'll freeze the structure.

We do so at the expense of our dark-squared bishop, but we are controlling the one pawn break that can change everything.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2pp4/8/1P2P3/PBPP1P.text:
If Black develops to c6. Black might have plans that include ...e5.

We don't want them to have three pawns in the center.

You can pin that knight right away.

Now ...e5 is impossible.

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3p4/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP.text:
The most common move at this point is 2...Nc6, played 22% of the time.

Black might want ...e5, but now we don't have to allow it.

In this move order, we can prevent both pawns from reaching the center.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/3p4/2PP2b1/1P2PN2.text:
If Black castles, we can choose where to develop the queenside knight.

I suggest c3, since it's slightly more active and pressures the d5-square.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/8/2PP2b1/4PN2/PB2.text:
And so will we.

Next, we'll attack the bishop with h3 and develop our knight to d2.

We can consider c5 and Nc4 at some point.

r2qk2r/p4ppp/2pbpn2/2pp4/8/1P1PP3/PBP2PP.text:
The way to play against this is the slow build-up with d3, Nd2 and eventually e4 to challenge the center.

We can also play f4 and Qf3 to further expand and improve.

r2qk2r/p4ppp/2pbpn2/2pp4/8/1P2P3/PBPP1PP.text:
The pawn recaptures.

Black does have a solid structure, but their c-pawns are doubled.

r2qk2r/pp1nbppp/2p1pnb1/3p4/2P4N/1P2P3/P.text:
Black supports the center.

We have to come up with a plan to finish development.

I suggest d3 with the idea of Nd2, as it also undermines Black's bishop on g6.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2bbpn2/2ppN3/8/1P2P3/PBPP1.text:
Black allows the capture on c6 and develops the bishop first.

We'll take.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/3p4/3P2b1/1P2PN2/P.text:
Black prepares castling.

And we'll play c4, of course.

This can never be a bad move if Black has a knight on c6 and can't play ...c6 to support the center.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/8/2pP2b1/1P2PN2/PB.text:
Black taking on c4 only helps us.

We'll recapture with the pawn and now we've got a lot more space in the center.

r2qk2r/pppnbppp/4pnb1/3p4/7N/1P2P3/PBPPB.text:
In fact, our playstyle will probably prompt Black to castle long and discourage us from capturing on g6 at all.

In response to Black's plans, let's play actively in the center.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2n1pn2/1Bpp4/8/1P2PN2/P.text:
Once Black commits their pawn to ...e6, it means we've succeeded in preventing ...e5.

Now we can take control of the e5-square.

We'll trade on c6 first.

r2qkb1r/pp1bpppp/2n2n2/1Bpp4/8/1P2PN2/PB.text:
Black could "give up" on this plan and continue development.

We'll just castle.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2b1pn2/2pp4/8/1P2PN2/PBPP.text:
With an obvious active central move once Black recaptures.

And that's Ne5.

r2qkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/3p4/6b1/1P2PN2/PB.text:
If Black doesn't want to block their bishop, they can activate it to g4.

The threat of ...e5 is reintroduced, so we'll stop it with d4 this time.

We'll play for c4 as well.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P2b1/1P2PN2/.text:
Black has to settle for ...e6.

Let's unpin first and bring our knight back to life.

r2qkbnr/1p1bpppp/p1n5/1Bpp4/8/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
Black can be persistent and attack our bishop with ...a6.

In that case, we'll capture.

r2qkbnr/1p2pppp/p1b5/2pp4/8/1P2PN2/PBPP1.text:
Once this trade happens and Black recaptures with the bishop...

Most of the time, you can instinctively place your knight on e5 and attack that bishop.

r2qkbnr/pp1bpppp/2n5/1Bpp4/8/1P2P3/PBPP1.text:
Black unpins.

You don't have to rush capturing on c6 yet.

Nf3 simply stops ...e5.

r2qr1k1/ppp2ppp/2nbpn2/3p4/2PP2b1/1PN1PN.text:
And we'll get out of the way.

We've got an easy plan with h3 incoming to attack the bishop on g4.

Our rook is coming to the c-file which might open up at some point if trades occur.

You can even consider Nb5 with the idea of Nxd6 at some point in the future.

r3k1r1/1p3pbp/p1q1p3/2pp4/8/1P1PPQ2/P1P2.text: Black can exert more pressure on the diagonal.

r3k1r1/1p3pbp/p1q1p3/2pp4/8/1PPPPQ2/P4PP.text:
It does force us to play c3 and block, thus worsening our pawn structure.

But I'd take this position up a pawn any day.

One of the ways to untangle is to castle, bring the h-rook to c1 and then play Nd2.

Another one is to play for d4.

r3k2r/ppqnbppp/2p1pnb1/3p4/2P4N/1P1PP3/P.text:
Black will prepare queenside castling.

And we'll activate the knight.

Standard.

r3kb1r/1p3p1p/p1q1pp2/2pp4/8/1P1PPQ2/P1P.text:
Black recaptures.

And loses a pawn.

The only compensation they have...

r3kb1r/1p3ppp/p1q1pn2/2pp4/8/1P1PPQ2/PBP.text:
The queen recaptures.

Now the knight on f6 is under attack twice.

So we'll take it.

r3kb1r/1pq1pppp/p1b2n2/2ppN3/8/1P2PQ2/PB.text:
Black finally develops the kingside knight.

With our queen out, an alternative to the line we'll show here is g4.

It's an active move that aims to dislodge the Black knight from its post on f6.

A safer option is d3, awaiting Black's next move.

r3kb1r/1pq2ppp/p1b1pn2/2ppN3/8/1P1PPQ2/P.text:
And once ...e6 arrives, you can actually win a pawn here!

We can trade on c6 first.

r3kbnr/1pq1pppp/p1b5/2ppN3/8/1P2P3/PBPP1.text:
It doesn't necessarily mean we'll capture if Black allows us to.

We can wait and take at the right time.

Let's bring the queen into the game with some pressure in the center.

r3kbr1/1p3p1p/p1q1pQ2/2pp4/8/1P1PP3/P1P2.text:
Are the open g-file and the long diagonal.

But Qf3 easily takes care of the g2-pawn.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p1b2/8/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
Black does the same.

Let's spice things up before we castle.

And attack the bishop on f5.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bppp/4pnb1/3p4/7N/1P2P3/PBPP.text:
Black retreats to g6.

It's important to delay the capture on g6 for now, because we don't want to open up the h-file for Black.

We should wait for them to castle kingside first. So we'll just castle.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/8/1P2P3/PBPP.text:
A unique setup is 3...Bf5, or the Reverse London.

Against this approach, I would recommend standard development and jumping to the king's knight to h4 at some point to attack the active bishop.

We'll bring the knight to f3 first.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/8/1P2PN2/PBP.text:
As mentioned, Black connects the pawns on light squares.

We'll prepare castling.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2pp4/5P2/1P1BPN2/P.text:
Expect Black to advance with ...c5 at some point anyway.

Let's just castle and reevaluate the position entering the middlegame.

We've got the active bishops and a clamp on the e5-square, while Black has a bigger central presence with the pawns.

We are looking at the e5-square.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/5P2/1P2PN2/PB.text:
Black castles.

The d3-square is most active for our bishop.

There is no danger of ...e5 and ...e4, so there's no need for us to place the bishop on e2.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/5P2/1P2P3/PBPP.text:
Black prepares castling now.

And we'll continue normal development, too.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP.text:
Black activates the kingside knight first 17% of the time.

Still keeping it flexible.

Of course, e3 is a no-brainer for us.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/8/1P2P3/PBPP1P.text:
There are many setups for both sides after 3...e6, but the obvious disadvantage is that Black blocks the light-squared bishop.

When you see a pawn chain on a certain color complex in the center, it's usually a good idea to play on the other one.

Which is why f4 makes a lot of sense.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP/R.text:
A move that goes together with ...d5 is ...c5, and it's played 16% of the time in this position.

Black takes as much central space as possible in Queen's Gambit style.

As always, e3 is a strong response.

We open up our light-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/8/1P6/P1PPPPPP/R.text:
Black pushes ...d5 in 25% of online games. That's more than 20 million games with this move. 

Black gives us the dark squares but retains flexibility and keeps us guessing which plan they'll go for.

We'll fianchetto anyway.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Chapter 4 will deal with the first deviation on move 1, and that's 1...d5.

Black doesn't have to place the pawn on e5 which can become a target and can choose to push the d-pawn first, keeping it safe on a light square.

This grabs central space just as much as ...e5, so it's definitely worth exploring.

r1b2rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/q7/3Q4/1PN1PP2/PB.text:
We'll simply slide the king to b1 and protect the pawn, with e4 ideas.

Don't be afraid of the knight discoveries. You can always retreat to d2.

If Black jumps to d5, you can even play Nxd5 and sacrifice the queen!

They develop the queen to a5 instead.

There is some pressure on the a2-pawn and the knight on c3.

r1bq1rk1/p2pppbp/2p2np1/8/8/1P2P3/PBP1BP.text:
Black castles.

And so will we.

Once the kings are away, Black will probably shift their focus towards the center.

r1bq1rk1/p3bppp/2pp1n2/4p3/2P5/1P2P3/PB2.text:
But our king is safe as well.

Our plan will be simple and straightforward: we'll develop the knight to the c3-square and bring the queen to c2 with a light-squared presence.

Our rooks can go to c1 and d1.

r1bq1rk1/p3ppbp/2p2np1/3p4/8/1P2P3/PBP1B.text:
And play a move like ...d5.

This should ring alarm bells for you to challenge their structure right away.

And there's no better way to do that than c4.

r1bq1rk1/p4pbp/2p1pnp1/3p4/2P5/1P2P3/PB2.text: At the very least, this will probably induce Black to block their light-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/p4pbp/2p1pnp1/3p4/2P5/1P2P3/PBQ.text:
In the meantime, we can slide our queen away from the d-file and prepare to slide a rook there, lining up with Black's queen.

Apart from that, our knight is flexible to develop to either d2 or c3, with the queenside rook coming to the c-file which might open at some point.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pppbp/5np1/8/3Q4/1PN1P3/PBP2.text:
Black castles short.

Will we do the same?

Nope! Let's castle on opposite sides.

This usually means that there will be a lot of fireworks on the board.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3Q4/1PN1P3/PBP.text:
Black pushes ...d6. What now?

I like a pawn on e4, so let's play f3 to prepare it.

Our queen is great on d4 and we should keep it there for as long as possible.

Black can't play ...e5 for now because of the d6-pawn.

r1bqk2r/p2pppbp/2p2np1/8/8/1P2P3/PBP2PPP.text:
The b-pawn recaptures.

It's time to complete development now.

r1bqk2r/p3bppp/2pp1n2/4p3/2P5/1P2P3/PB3P.text:
Black prepares castling...

And so do we.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/8/3N4/1P2P3/PBP2.text:
If Black doesn't trade but develops...

We'll be the ones who trade!

We don't want any shenanigans on the long diagonal.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/5np1/8/3Q4/1P2P3/PBP2PP.text:
Black goes for the fianchetto.

They are threatening ...Nh5, so we have to be a bit careful.

We'll activate the knight on c3 and block the diagonal for a moment.

r1bqkb1r/p3pp1p/2pp1np1/8/8/1P4P1/PBP1PP.text:
To fight against at least one of the bishops, Black wants to fianchetto as well.

We'll develop the bishop to g2 and attack the pawn.

r1bqkb1r/p3pppp/2pp1n2/8/8/1P6/PBP1PPPP/.text:
Black recaptures.

Our idea is to fianchetto the light-squared bishop as well!

Whichever pawn Black wants to push and undermine one of the bishops, it makes the other one stronger.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2pp1n2/4p3/2P5/1P6/PB2PPP.text:
Black activates the knight instead...

And we'll continue naturally.

No need to fianchetto here when Black already has a pawn on e5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/2n2np1/2p5/8/1P2PN2/PB.text:
And Black goes for the fianchetto.

This is a strong plan because Black has a pawn on c5 which is limiting our central playability.

We'll go for d4 anyway! What's our plan?

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/2n2np1/8/3p4/1P2PN2/PB.text:
Well, once Black captures on d4...

I suggest we recapture with the knight and keep our bishop open.

This trade activated our knight in the center and removed Black's annoying c5-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/8/3n4/1P2P3/PBP2P.text:
Black can certainly trade on d4.

But that gives us even more space on the diagonal.

We'll recapture with the queen, and this battery looks scary.

Also, we can choose to castle queenside now.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n2n2/2p5/8/1P3N2/PBPP.text:
3...Nf6 is played 25% of the time in this position.

The Two Knights setup is viable independently of what Black plays as the first move.

However, in this case, Black probably wants to fianchetto on g7 and undermine our bishop on b2.

Our e3 idea is also never a mistake.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2np1n2/8/3N4/1P6/PBP1PP.text:
The most common move is Black developing on f6 and choosing calm development instead of the fierce ...e5.

I actually recommend we trade here.

You will see why.

r1bqkbnr/p4ppp/2pp4/4p3/8/1P6/PBP1PPPP/R.text:
We do bring Black's pawns back together in the center...

But we'll make sure they can't play ...d5 that easily!

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP.text:
Black activates the knight to c6.

We don't have to allow ...e5.

So let's stop it.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/2p5/8/1P3N2/PBPPPP.text:
Black goes for ...d6 and connects the pawn chain 20% of the time.

This reintroduces the ...e5 idea, so we'll try to prevent it with d4.

The problem is, if Black is persistent, they can achieve ...e5 by force.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/8/3p4/1P3N2/PBP1PP.text:
Black captures. 

This is where 1...c5 comes in handy.

We'll recapture with the knight.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2np4/4p3/3N4/1P6/PBP1PPP.text:
If Black wants to be aggressive, you should be prepared to face the sharp ...e5.

Our knight is under attack and retreating would only give Black the momentum.

Let's trade instead.

r2qk2r/p2bppbp/2pp1np1/8/2P5/1P4P1/PB2PP.text:
Well, c4 is an easy choice.

We can even play e4 together with it to get a clamp on the d5-square.

Apart from that, we'll play Nc3, Qc2 and bring the rooks to d1 and e1 to improve.

A comfortable position for White.

r2qk2r/p2bppbp/2pp1np1/8/8/1P4P1/PBP1PPB.text: How will we stop Black's idea after they fianchetto?

r2qkb1r/p2bpp1p/2pp1np1/8/8/1P4P1/PBP1PP.text:
Black defends, but passively.

It would be ideal for them if they could play ...Bg7 and ...d5, improving on both color complexes.

We'll castle for now.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/8/1P6/P1PPPPPP/R.text:
Black responds with ...c5 about 7% of the time, and it was seen in almost 5.5 million games.

Black controls the d4-square without committing the e-pawn to e5 and potentially making it a target.

Also, Black moves the c-pawn before developing the knight to c6.

Our second move stays the same, of course.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
We've looked at Black playing 1...e5 and 1...d5, so it's only suitable we take a look at 1...c5 by Black in Chapter 5.

We'll cover some lines that have independent value against our approach, such as the ...c5 and ...d6 setup or the ...c5 and ...Nf6 setup.

Let's go.

r1b2rk1/pp3pbp/2n2pp1/q1p5/8/1PN1P1P1/P2.text:
The knight comes out to c6...

And we'll castle.

Even though Black has prevented d4, there's no danger to the position.

r1br2k1/pp3pbp/2n2pp1/q1p5/8/1PN1P1P1/P2.text:
The rook slides to d8 to exert pressure on the d-file.

We don't want to allow something like ...Nb4 and ...Nd3.

r1br2k1/pp3pbp/2n2pp1/q1p5/8/PPN1P1P1/3P.text:
So we will play a3 to stop that.

Since we can't play d4, we can undermine Black's position by playing on the light squares.

Our bishop on g2 is strong, and we can look to dominate the d5-square with Nf4 and Nfd5. 

The queen could improve on c2.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1pbp/2ppb1p1/5p2/2P5/1PN1P1P.text: And once the knight gets out...

r2q1rk1/pp1n1pbp/2ppb1p1/5p2/2PP4/1PN1P1.text:
We'll play it. If Black goes for ...Nf6, we can even play d5.

The computer claims we have a really small advantage but I would argue that this position is much easier to play for White with the central presence and space.

Our pieces are placed perfectly and we are ready to castle as well.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pbp/2ppb1p1/5p2/2P5/1PN1P1P1.text:
Black activates the bishop.

And we'll get the knight out first.

Developing comfortably and preparing d4.

rnb1k2r/ppp2pbp/5pp1/3q4/8/1P2P3/P2P1PPP.text:
Black goes for the fianchetto.

Let's develop with tempo now and block the diagonal.

We don't want to give Black too much activity.

rnb1k2r/ppp2pbp/5pp1/q7/8/1PN1P3/P2P1PPP.text:
Black can stick around and keep some pressure on our knight. This is designed to stop d4.

That's fine, as our g-knight coming to e2 will support it.

We can go ahead and prepare the fianchetto.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2p1p/5pp1/3q4/8/1P6/P2PPPPP/.text:
The queen recaptures.

We don't want to give Black too much space.

It's crucial to play on the dark squares quickly since we've weakened the diagonal.

So we will play e3, leaving our options open for d4 at some point.

rnb2rk1/pp3pbp/5pp1/q1p5/8/1PN1P1P1/P2P1.text:
Black takes more control of the square.

But we will support the knight.

We are ready to castle on the next move.

rnb2rk1/ppp2pbp/5pp1/q7/8/1PN1P1P1/P2P1P.text:
Apart from ...f5, their plans could revolve around ...c5 and ...Nc6 which we will demonstrate here.

Instead of developing the knight to d7, Black wants to prevent d4 by playing this way.

We will still activate the bishop. Our setup is solid enough even without d4.

rnbq1rk1/pp1p1pbp/2p3p1/5p2/2P5/1PN3P1/P.text:
And Black goes for the expected setup.

They don't want to allow our knight to jump to d5.

We'll fianchetto. Black is not playing ...d5 anytime soon.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2pp2p1/5p2/2P5/1PN3P1/P2.text:
Instead, they settle for ...d6, as they want to activate the bishop to e6.

A classic battle in the center.

Since we've basically secured the d5-square, it's time to expand ourselves.

Black has done nothing to prevent d4, so that's what we are going for.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/5pp1/8/8/1PN1P1P1/P2P1P.text:
Black castles, with the idea of finally playing ...f5.

And we'll fianchetto.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/6p1/5p2/8/1PN1P1P1/P2PN.text:
We can simply continue developing, with an equal position.

We can play d4 and castle next.

rnbq1rk1/pppp1pbp/5pp1/8/2P5/1PN5/P2PPPP.text:
Black will castle.

And we'll go for the idea I mentioned.

It's also effective because with the pawn on c4, we can utilize the full power of the bishop on g2.

rnbq1rk1/pppp1pbp/6p1/5p2/2P5/1PN3P1/P2P.text:
Black opens up the bishop.

Why should we leave our knight pinned on c3?

Let's unpin and protect it.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pbp/5pp1/8/8/1PN1P3/P2P1PPP/.text:
If the queen retreats to d8, we can implement the double fianchetto approach we want.

The bishop is coming to g2.

rnbqk2r/pppp1pbp/5pp1/8/2P5/1P6/P2PPPPP/.text:
You will see ...Bg7 as often as 85% of the time, as it is a move that plays itself.

Black's main ideas will revolve around ...f5 and ...c6 with ...d6.

On the other hand, our approach will be to fianchetto the light-squared bishop as well!

First, let's develop and block the diagonal.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5pp1/3p4/2P5/1P6/P2PPPP.text:
Going for ...d5 right away is the top engine move but is extremely rare at amateur level, being played only 4% of the time.

Players simply don't like to place a pawn on d5 and commit to a trade when we play c4.

If this happens, capturing in the center is the way to go.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5pp1/8/8/1P6/P1PPPPPP/.text:
Black has to recapture with the e-pawn.

And we will play c4 already to take some control of the center.

One option Black has is ...c6, against which the best course of action is e3 and developing the knights to c3 and f3.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP/.text:
Blocking with the knight is the most natural, and here's a surprising move already.

We give up the bishop, but we will double Black's pawns and will use the time they need to untangle and play ...f5 to expand in the center.

Usually we are the ones who give up the center after 1.b3, but this time we will be taking it!

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/8/1P6/P1PPPPPP/R.text:
Black counters with ...g6.

This is played 4% of the time, in more than 1.2 million games.

We will attack the rook.

Black won't fianchetto and blunder, unless they premove.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Chapter 6 will show you what to do against Black's g6 setups.

A lot of players like to counter our early fianchetto with a fianchetto of their own, thinking that's the most natural way to contest the diagonal.

It certainly could be a sound plan, but our strategy is actually to capture the knight on f6 and give up the bishop!

You will see why.
